title: The Swamp Can’t Win Your Vote, So Washington Wants To Buy It
text:
(Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)

American politics used to host lively debates about policy, priorities, and the future of our nation. Americans were not bitterly divided; we didn’t look down in disgust at our neighbors who disagreed with who we thought ought to be in the White House. Nevertheless, at some point in the last few decades, we lost any semblance of the tame system that once characterized our political apparatus. Instead, it has been replaced with partisan politics hyper-focused on social issues that affect the few, while forgetting the many.

The ineffectiveness of this political machine is evident; it is difficult to find a better encapsulation of the state of our politics than the bipartisan push to simply pay for votes. Gone are the days of actually running campaigns, policy platforms, or diplomacy; the political overlords have sunk the economy, driven up costs, and cheered on sky-high inflation, but worry not, in return they have humbly offered to pay for your vote.

As the chosen few deprive the American economy and abandon the average man, leaving him struggling to afford food, pay for an education, own property, or start a family. The powerful are busy chasing their own egotistical political aspirations and bowing to special interests willing to line their campaign coffers so they can tighten their grip around the jugular of our union. And to maintain their power? Graciously return some of that cash back to the people, in exchange for your vote, of course.

President Donald Trump unveiled the Republican Party’s grand plan at its midterm convention in Dallas. Amid talk of the Iran war and America’s supposed “Golden Age,” Trump offered perhaps his most ambitious proposal yet: If Republicans retain control of the House and Senate, every adult American would receive a $5,000 “dividend.” At roughly 240 million eligible adults, the proposal would cost around $1.2 trillion, and neither Trump nor his administration has provided a clear funding mechanism. Tariff revenue, one potential source floated by the administration, would fall far short of covering the bill.

So, after years of Washington spending trillions of dollars and watching inflation erode Americans’ purchasing power, the answer is apparently to send everyone another check.

Trump’s proposal has predictably drawn Democratic accusations that Republicans are trying to buy votes. But Democrats might want to be careful about throwing stones from inside the same pigpen.

A Townhall investigation published Wednesday featured Sky McAdams, an organizing manager for Texas Majority PAC, describing a program that pays voters $25 to participate in a one-hour Zoom class about voting and political organizing. McAdams himself described the arrangement as “a roundabout way of paying people for their votes.” Townhall reported that the program, operated by Relentless through its Rally software, is designed to recruit, persuade, and mobilize voters. Texas Majority PAC reported paying Relentless $500,000 for a “relational organizing program” in July.

Tammany Hall, New York’s infamous political machine, built its power in part through patronage, providing jobs and assistance to loyal constituents while cultivating political loyalty at the ballot box. Boss Tweed’s machine became synonymous with corruption, and the Tweed Ring openly bought votes and used patronage to maintain its political power. (RELATED: Republicans Promised To Put America First, Instead They’ve Betrayed Everyone For Money From Massive Agriculture Donors)

The machinery today is more sophisticated. The transaction is not.

All in all, Washington has decided you, the American voter, no longer require half-decent ideas, a plan for the future, or any alignment with the policies being proposed; no, all it takes is some cash. And the political apparatus has got plenty of it.

That is what makes this moment so dispiriting. A republic is supposed to ask citizens to judge competing visions for their country. Politicians are supposed to make the case that their policies will improve Americans’ lives. Instead, we are increasingly watching political campaigns approach voters as consumers: Find out what they want, put a price tag on it, and make the sale.

And where does that logic end?

If $5,000 can be dangled in front of voters, why not $10,000? If one group can be offered a benefit in exchange for its political support, why shouldn’t every other group demand one as well?

An election should not become an auction in which politicians compete to see who can offer the most attractive payout.

The irony is particularly difficult to ignore when Americans are already struggling with the cost of living. Washington has spent years arguing over taxes, spending, subsidies, and economic policy while ordinary Americans have watched the prices of necessities climb, and the cost of housing, education, and raising a family become increasingly difficult to manage. Now, instead of offering a convincing plan to address those problems, politicians can simply promise to send some money back and ask voters to remember them at the ballot box.

A voter should be able to look at a candidate and ask: What do you believe? What will you do with power? How will your policies affect my family, my community, and my country?

The answer shouldn’t be a dollar amount.

Your vote is not a coupon. It is not a loyalty reward. It is not something politicians should be able to purchase with a check drawn from the public treasury or a payment dressed up as political organizing.

The last thing we need is politicians waging a bidding war for the electorate. We need politicians willing to make their case to the electorate.

Disgusted is a bit of an understatement; regardless of what you think about the war in Iran, men in women’s sports, or abortion, Americans should be able to recognize the larger problem staring them in the face: a political establishment acting in the interests of those who control it rather than those it is supposed to serve. The capital’s political class has decided that the easiest way to win your support is not to earn it, but to put a price on it.

Your vote is worth more than that. It should never be for sale.
